entries.line: In John often the Judean authorities in Jerusalem; sometimes the crowds, or simply the people. Never a verdict on a whole people (1:19, 4:22).
What Elijah heard at Horeb after the wind, the earthquake and the fire (19:12). Translations vary: a gentle whisper, or a sound of thin silence.
Aramaic for ‘Father’, the word Jesus uses as he prays in the garden (14:36).
The Aramaic word for father, used by Jesus (Mark 14:36). The Spirit leads Gentile believers to pray it too (4:6).
To remain, stay, live in. John's word for a lasting bond with Jesus, like a branch in a vine (15:4).
Christ ‘has abolished death’ (1:10): not taken it out of human life, but broken its power.
Greek orthotomeō, to cut straight, as a road or a furrow. Keeping a straight course with God's word (2:15).
Adam means ‘human being’ or ‘man’; adamah means ‘ground’. The man is formed from the ground (2:7), and to the ground he returns (3:19).
Greek huiothesia, being made a son and heir. By the Spirit every believer, woman or man, is God's child and heir (8:15-17).
Greek paraklētos: one called alongside to help, plead for and comfort. John's name for the Holy Spirit (14:26).
Greek paraklētos, one called alongside to speak for another. Here it is Jesus, before the Father (2:1).
In Hebrew Shaddai, a name for God linked with his power. Naomi uses it twice in her complaint (1:20-21).
‘So be it’, a word of faithfulness; one of Christ's titles (3:14).
Those who left their proper dwelling, held for judgment (1:6).
In Hebrew mashiach, someone set apart by having oil poured on the head. Hannah's prayer is the first place it names a king (2:10). It gives English messiah, and its Greek form is Christ.

In Hebrew mashiach, someone set apart by having oil poured on the head. David condemns the man who claimed to have killed the LORD's anointed (1:14), and his song ends with God's love for ‘His anointed’ (22:51). Its Greek form is Christ.
Hebrew mashiach, from which ‘Messiah’ comes; Greek christos, ‘Christ’. First the king anointed with oil (Psalm 2:2); for Christians, Jesus.
Greek chrisma. Most read it as the Holy Spirit given to all believers; some, as the gospel they received (2:20, 27).
One who opposes Christ or puts a false Christ in his place. In John, teachers who deny the Son (2:18, 22; 4:3).
One who opposes Christ or puts a false Christ in his place; here, teachers who deny he came in the flesh (1:7).
A kind of ancient book that shows heaven's view of history through visions and symbols.
One who is sent. In Acts mostly the Twelve, who had been with Jesus and saw him risen (1:21-22); Paul and Barnabas are also called apostles (14:14).
Paul could order but chooses to ask, ‘on the basis of love’ (verses 8-10).
Greek epiphaneia, the source of ‘epiphany’. Used for a god showing himself or a ruler arriving (2:13).
Greek dokimos, tested and found genuine, like metal or a full-weight coin (2:15).
A chief angel. Michael, who also appears in Daniel (1:9).
‘Numbers’, the name given to the book in the old Greek translation, after the two counts of the people (chapters 1 and 26).
The gold-covered chest that stood for God's presence, called by the name of the LORD of Hosts, ‘who is enthroned between the cherubim’ (6:2).
The gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law and was the sign of God's presence. It goes ahead of Israel into the Jordan (3:3).
The gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the covenant. Its lid was seen as the throne of the LORD, ‘who sits enthroned between the cherubim’ (4:4).
Truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the word of God, and prayer (6:13-18), taken from Isaiah's picture of God himself.
The guilt offering, for wrongs that did damage. It came with repayment and a fifth added (5:14-6:7).
Greek epaischunomai. The key word of chapter 1 (1:8, 12, 16). Prison was a public disgrace, shared by the prisoner's friends.
A Canaanite goddess, and the wooden pole that stood for her at shrines (14:23; 16:33).
A Canaanite goddess, and the wooden pole that stood for her. Manasseh set up a carved Asherah pole in the temple (21:7).
Goddesses worshiped beside Baal. Israel served them too (2:13; 3:7).
Greek hilastērion (3:25), the BSB's ‘atoning sacrifice’, with ‘propitiation’ in its footnote. In the Greek Old Testament the same word names the mercy seat on the ark.
Greek hilasmos, the sacrifice that deals with sin and turns away judgment (2:2; 4:10).
The right and power to act. Jesus has it to teach, to cast out spirits, and to forgive sins (1:22, 2:10).
To work or serve. The same word is used for slavery to Pharaoh and for the worship of God. Exodus is a change of masters.
The near relative whose duty it was, in the ancient world, to pursue the one who had killed a member of the family (20:3).
The word for where the second goat was sent (16:8). Its meaning is uncertain; older Bibles give ‘scapegoat’.
Lord or master, the Canaanite storm god said to send the rain. Ahab built him a temple in Samaria (16:32).
Baal was the storm god of Canaan, believed to bring the rain and the harvest. ‘The Baals’ are his local forms and shrines (2:11).
The god worshiped at Peor, on the heights above the plains of Moab, where Israel fell into idolatry (25:3).
The great city opposed to God; many read it first as Rome (17:5, 18).
To create. In the Bible only God does this. It appears 53 times in the Old Testament, 11 of them in Genesis, first in 1:1.
A power that demands worship, drawn from Daniel's beasts (13:1).
To trust, to come to Jesus and stay with him. John uses the verb 98 times and the noun ‘faith’ not once (20:31).
‘In the wilderness’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first sentence (1:1).
Blessing. God's first word to people is a blessing (1:28), and his call to Abraham repeats it again and again (12:1-3).
Hebrew ‘in the beginning’, the first word of the Bible and the Hebrew name of the book. John's Gospel opens with the same words (John 1:1).
Covenant: a binding promise that makes a lasting bond. It appears 27 times in Genesis, first with Noah (6:18) and then with Abraham.
The Hebrew amanah, a firm commitment, from the root of amen. The people put their pledge in writing and seal it (9:38).
Hebrew ashre, the first word of the book. Not a passing mood but a whole life that is going well under God: ‘how happy’, ‘how rich in good’.
Greek kauchaomai, to boast, to take pride. More than half of its uses in the New Testament are in this letter. Paul's rule: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (10:17).
Greek sōma. The believer's own body, a temple of the Spirit (6:19); the church, the body of Christ (12:27); and the body that will be raised (15:44).
The church as Christ's body, many members with one head (1:22-23; 4:15-16).
Greek parrēsia, open and free speech without fear (4:13, 4:29). The last word of Acts describes Paul preaching ‘boldly’ (28:31).
The scroll found in the temple in Josiah's eighteenth year (22:8), called the Book of the Covenant when he reads it to the people (23:2). Many scholars connect it with Deuteronomy.
The Hebrew sukkot, shelters of branches. Israel lived in them at the Feast of Tabernacles to remember the wilderness years (8:14-17).
Greek anagennaō, to give new birth, found in the New Testament only in 1 Peter (1:3, 23).
Greek anōthen, which means both ‘again’ and ‘from above’: a new birth whose source is God (3:3, 3:7).
Shame. Saul's son Ish-bosheth and Jonathan's son Mephibosheth are called Eshbaal and Merib-baal in 1 Chronicles; scribes seem to have put this word in place of baal.
Greek oikodomeō, to build a house. Paul's test for knowledge, gifts and worship: does it build up the church? (8:1; 14:26).
Greek apseudēs, found only here (1:2). Set against the Cretan saying of 1:12.
Greek pherō, used in Acts of a ship driven by the wind: the prophets moved by the Spirit (1:21).
Greek harpazō, to snatch up suddenly. The Latin Bible's word here gives English the word ‘rapture’ (4:17). The word itself says nothing about timing.
Elisha's cry as Elijah is taken (2:12), and the king's cry over the dying Elisha (13:14): the prophet was Israel's real defense.
The sin offering, which many scholars call the purification offering. It dealt with wrongs done without meaning to and with some uncleanness (4:1-35).
Winged guardian figures of God's throne. Two great ones, carved of olive wood and covered with gold, spread their wings in the inner room (6:23-28).
Loving devotion: loyal, covenant love that goes beyond what is owed. God names it as his own in 34:6-7.
Greek archipoimēn, found only here in the New Testament: Christ, to whom elders answer (5:4).
Greek kuria, ‘lady’. A church, or a woman who led one; kuria may also be a name (1:1).
God's choosing and his deciding beforehand (1:4-5, 11). Christians read these words in more than one way; see the part above.
Greek for Messiah, ‘anointed one’: the king Israel was waiting for (1:1, 8:29).
A name first given to the disciples at Antioch (11:26); in Acts it is used by outsiders (26:28).
Greek Christianos, a follower of Christ, one of only three uses in the New Testament (4:16).
In Greek ekklesia, ‘assembly’. Matthew is the only Gospel to use it (16:18, 18:17).
Greek ekklēsia, an assembly or gathering. The word Acts uses for the believers together (5:11, 8:1).
A picture of a heart changed toward God. Israel is told to do it (10:16), and God promises to do it for them (30:6).
The sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17). The teachers in Galatia said Gentile believers must receive it. Paul says, “neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything” (6:15).
Greek politeuma, the state you belong to. In a Roman colony Paul says “our citizenship is in heaven” (3:20).
One of six towns where a person who had killed someone by accident could flee and be heard before anyone took revenge (35:11).
One of six towns where a person who had killed by accident was safe until the case was heard (20:2-3).
Hebrew taher, to be clean: fit to come near. The priest's word ‘clean’ brought a person back into the full life of the people (13:17; 14:20).
The sign of God's presence over the tabernacle, cloud by day and the look of fire by night. Israel moved only when it lifted (9:15-23).
Greek paraklēsis, strength given by one who comes alongside. With its verb it comes more often in this letter than in any other book of the New Testament. God is “the God of all comfort” (1:3).
Greek parousia, a ruler's arrival; used for Christ's return (3:4, 12).
The Hebrew rachamim, related to the word for womb. The great prayer gives it as the reason Israel still exists: in God's great compassion he did not forsake them (9:19, 27, 28, 31).
A wife of lower standing, bound to a man but without the full place of a first wife (19:1).
A wife of lower rank. Taking a ruler's concubines could be a claim to his place, which is why Abner's act (3:7) and Absalom's (16:22) were acts of power.
Greek homologeō, to say the same thing: to agree with God about sin, or about Jesus (1:9; 4:2).
Greek syneidēsis, the inner sense that judges your own actions. A ‘weak’ conscience is one still troubled by its old life with idols; others must not wound it (8:7-12).
The inner sense that judges your own conduct. Throw away a good conscience and faith runs aground (1:19).
Greek epagōnizomai, to struggle hard, as in an athletic contest. Only here in the New Testament (1:3).
Greek autarkēs, a word the Stoic teachers prized. Paul's contentment comes from Christ who strengthens him (4:11-13).
Greek autarkeia, a word the Stoic teachers prized. For Paul, contentment rests in God, who provides (6:6-8).
The earthly tabernacle was real, but it pointed to something greater, as a shadow points to what casts it (8:5; 10:1).
In Hebrew etsah, advice. Ahithophel's counsel was ‘like the consultation of the word of God’ (16:23), and the LORD defeated it (17:14).
Not merit earned, but a life that fits the calling God gives, by his grace (1:5, 11-12).
Hebrew berit, a binding, sworn relationship with promises and duties on both sides. Sealed with blood at Sinai (24:8).
A binding relationship with promises and duties. Deuteronomy sets out the covenant between the LORD and Israel (5:2; 29:1).
A binding relationship with promises and duties. At Shechem Israel renews its covenant with the LORD (24:25).
In Hebrew berit, a binding agreement sealed by oath. David makes one with the elders of Israel (5:3), and his last words call God's promise ‘an everlasting covenant’ (23:5).
Greek diathēkē, a binding relationship with promises and duties. In ordinary Greek it could also mean a will (8:6; 9:16).
Israel's cry to God in distress, which again and again moved him to send help (3:9; 10:10).
The most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels. Paul calls his message “the message of the cross” (1:18): foolish to the world, God's power to those being saved.
Greek stephanos, the wreath given to a winning athlete, not a king's crown (4:8).
The royal servant who poured the king's wine and tasted it first. The post needed complete trust and gave daily access to the king (1:11).
The day Christ returns, when his work in his people is finished (1:6) and their bodies are made new (3:21).
The prophets' name for the day God acts to judge and to save. Paul ties it to the coming of Jesus (5:2).
The prophets' name for the day God acts to judge and to save. Some told the church it had already come (2:2).
Greek diakonos, servant. A recognized group in the church, chosen for character (3:8-13).
Greek planos, one who leads others astray (1:7).
The Aramaic chanukkah. The house of God was dedicated with joy (6:16). The same word later gave its name to Hanukkah, which remembers this temple's rededication in 164 BC.
The Hebrew chanukkah, the setting apart of the finished wall for God (12:27). The same word later named the feast of Hanukkah.
Greek apologia, a reasoned answer, as in a law court; the root of ‘apologetics’ (3:15).
The Berean Standard Bible's word for someone God raised up to save Israel from an enemy (3:9, 3:15).
Greek analusis, used of untying a boat or taking down a tent. A gentle word for death (4:6).
From a Greek word for a second law or a repetition of the law, taken from the old Greek translation of 17:18.
‘Words’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first line: ‘These are the words that Moses spoke’ (1:1).
The ban, in Hebrew herem: people or goods given over wholly to God, with nothing kept for human use (15:3).
The Berean Standard Bible's words for herem (6:17; 10:40).
A learner who follows a teacher. The last command is to make disciples of all nations (28:19).
The Hebrew cherpah, reproach. A ruined city shamed its people and the God whose name it bore. The wall was rebuilt so that the people would be a disgrace no longer (2:17).
Greek diaspora, the scattering: Jews living outside the land of Israel, or the church pictured as God's people far from home (1:1).
Greek theias phuseōs: sharing God's life by grace, never becoming God in essence (1:4).
Greek hairetikos, used only here. A person who makes factions, the later source of ‘heretic’ (3:10).
Greek poiētēs, one who does or makes. ‘Be doers of the word’ is the heart of chapter 1 (1:22-25).
Greek dipsuchos, literally ‘two-souled’: a heart divided between God and something else (1:8; 4:8).
A prayer of praise giving glory to God, like verses 24-25.
Greek pararreō, to flow past, like a boat slipping past its harbour. The danger is slow, not sudden (2:1).
Wine poured out at the altar with a sacrifice. Paul's picture of his coming death (4:6).
Stone of help. Samuel's name for the stone he set up after the victory at Mizpah: “Thus far the LORD has helped us” (7:12).
Hebrew ‘I am’ or ‘I will be’. God's name in 3:14 is ehyeh asher ehyeh, ‘I AM WHO I AM’; the same word promises ‘I will surely be with you’ (3:12).
Greek presbuteros. Leaders of the church; those who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve ‘double honor’ (5:17).
Greek presbuteros, an older man or a church leader. The writer's title (1:1).
Greek presbuteros, an older man or a church leader. The writer's title (1:1).
Greek presbuteros and episkopos. In Titus the same leaders, it seems (1:5, 7).
Greek presbuteroi, the recognised leaders of the congregation, called to pray over the sick (5:14).
‘Thousand’, but also a clan or a military unit (Judges 6:15). Behind the debate over the number who left Egypt (12:37).
Hebrew for ‘thousand’. It can also mean a clan or a military unit, which is why the census totals are read in more than one way (1:46).
Greek stoicheia: the building blocks of the world, or the sun, moon and stars (3:10, 12).
The usual Hebrew word for God. It is plural in form, but used of Israel's God it takes a singular verb: in 1:1 ‘God created’, not ‘they created’.
Greek kenoō. Christ ‘emptied Himself’ by taking the form of a servant (2:7), not by ceasing to be God.
The man from Colossae who brought the gospel home and now prays for the church (1:7; 4:12-13).
A garment worn by priests and used in seeking God's guidance. Gideon's gold ephod became a thing Israel worshiped (8:27).
A priestly garment used in asking God's guidance. Abiathar brought one with him when he fled to David (23:6, 9).
A linen garment worn by priests. David wore one as he danced before the ark (6:14).
An old name for Bethlehem or its clan. Naomi's family were Ephrathites (1:2; 4:11).
Greek olethros, ruin. Christians differ on whether it means unending loss or a final end, eternal in its effect (1:9).
Life with God that begins now and does not end: knowing the Father and the Son (3:16, 17:3).
Greek charaktēr, the mark a stamp or seal leaves, like the image on a coin. To see the Son is to see what God is (1:3).
Greek hupogrammos, a model of letters a child traces when learning to write (2:21).
Greek authenteō, used only here in the New Testament (2:12). Some read it as to lead or have authority; others as to domineer.
Being carried off from the land. Israel went to Assyria (17:6), and Judah to Babylon (24:14-16; 25:21).
In Hebrew golah, the exile or the body of exiles. It becomes a name for the returned community, the people carried away and brought back (1:11; 10:8).
Greek parepidēmoi, people living away from home. God's people whose true home is elsewhere (1:1; 2:11).
From the Greek exodos, a way out or departure. Luke uses the same word of Jesus' death in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).
Greek epoptēs, one who has seen with his own eyes (1:16).
‘A helper suitable for him’ (2:18). Of the word's 21 uses in the Old Testament, most describe God himself helping his people (Psalm 121:1-2). It does not mean a lesser rank.
Greek pistis, trust in God and his promise. The same word can mean faithfulness. Abraham is Paul's great example (4:3, 4:20-21).
Greek pistis, trust, and also faithfulness. Abraham “believed God” (3:6). Faith receives what God gives; it is not a new work to earn it.
The teaching ‘entrusted once for all to the saints’, received and handed on (1:3).
Greek anazōpureō, to stir up coals until they burn brightly. Gifts need tending (1:6).
Greek prosōpolēmpsia, literally ‘receiving the face’: judging people by how they look (2:1, 9).
Reverent awe that shapes behavior. Nehemiah gives it as the reason the nobles should stop exploiting the poor (5:9) and the reason he refused his allowance (5:15).
Greek synergos, one who works alongside. Those who support missionaries share their work (1:8).
Greek koinōnia, a shared life: with the Father and the Son, and so with one another (1:3, 7).
The heir, the one with first place. Christ is firstborn over creation and firstborn from the dead (1:15, 18), not a created being.
Greek sarx. The body or human descent (1:3), but often human nature turned from God and weak against sin (8:5-8).
Greek sarx. In Galatians not the body as such, but human nature turned in on itself, and human effort as a way to stand before God (3:3; 5:19).
In Hebrew mas, conscripted work for the king (5:13). The north's complaint against it split the kingdom (12:4, 18).
Greek paroikoi, resident aliens without citizenship, as Abraham was among the Hittites (2:11; compare 1:17).
In Hebrew olam, a long age. It comes eight times in chapter 7, set against Saul's short-lived line, and later readers took it at full strength.

words.word: Form of God, form of a servant

entries.line: Christ shared God's very nature, and took the nature of a servant as well (2:6-7). The same word ‘form’ is used of both.
The Hebrew Bible's name for Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, the history of Israel in its land.
The Hebrew yasad, to found, or to restore. Its range helps explain why the book and the prophets speak of the foundation being laid at different times (3:10; 5:16).
Greek archēgos, one who goes first and opens a way for others (2:10; 12:2).
Greek eleutheria. Freedom from slavery to the law's guardianship and to false gods, given for love: “serve one another in love” (5:13).
Greek eleutheria. The false teachers promise it while slaves to whatever masters them (2:19).
Greek philia, friendship that shares loyalties and enemies. Its only use in the New Testament (4:4).
To fill full, to bring to its goal. Matthew's word for how Jesus completes Israel's Scriptures (1:22, 5:17).
Greek plērōma. All God's fullness dwells in Christ (1:19; 2:9), and believers are made complete in him (2:10).
To redeem: to buy back a relative from slavery, as next of kin. God uses it of himself in 6:6: “I will redeem you with an outstretched arm”.
To redeem: to buy back a relative's land or freedom, the duty of the nearest of kin (25:25, 48-49).
Words from bookkeeping. Paul moves everything he was proud of into the loss column, for the sake of Christ (3:7-8).
The town's meeting place and court, where elders sat and agreements were made before witnesses (4:1).
The word behind ‘hell’ in 3:6, from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a name for the place of final judgment.
People who are not Jews. Acts is in large part the story of how they came to share in Israel's promises (10:45, 15:7-11).
Greek ethnē, the nations: everyone who is not Jewish. Paul was sent to bring them to faith (1:5), and Romans shows Jew and Gentile made one people (3:29-30).
The foreigner living among Israel, without land or family there. Israel is told to love him as itself (19:33-34).
Greek charisma, a gift of grace. Paul uses it for marriage and singleness (7:7) and for the gifts of the Spirit, given “for the common good” (12:7).
Israel's first camp in the land, near Jericho. The name sounds like the Hebrew verb for rolling: “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you” (5:9).
To gather the grain the reapers left behind, a right the law gave the poor, the foreigner and the widow (2:2).
In Hebrew kavod, from a word meaning heavy: the weight of God's presence. Ichabod's mother cried that the glory had departed from Israel (4:21).
In Hebrew kavod, weight, and so honor and the visible radiance of God's presence. It filled the house when the ark came in (8:11).
The weight and brightness of God's presence. John sees it in Jesus, and most of all at the cross (1:14, 17:1).
Greek doxa, the shining greatness of God. It shone on Moses' face (3:7), shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6), and is the “eternal weight of glory” still to come (4:17).
The redeemer, the nearest relative. In chapter 35 he is the ‘avenger of blood’, and the cities of refuge restrain him (35:12).
A title for the LORD in the Persian period, used in Cyrus's decree (1:2) and in the king's letter to Ezra (7:12, 21, 23).
Greek theopneustos, a rare word saying that Scripture is breathed out by God (3:16).
Greek eusebeia, reverence for God lived out in daily life. More common in these letters than anywhere else in the New Testament (4:7-8; 6:6).
Greek eusebeia, a word Greek moral teachers used for reverence; for Peter, a life shaped by God (1:3, 6-7).
Greek euangelizomai, to bring good news, the root of ‘gospel’ and ‘evangelist’. Luke's favourite verb for preaching (4:18, 8:1).
Good news. In Rome it announced a victory or a new emperor. Mark uses it for Jesus (1:1, 1:15).
Greek euangelion, good news. For Paul, the news about God's Son, promised beforehand in the Scriptures (1:1-4), which is God's power to save everyone who believes (1:16).
Greek euangelion, good news. Paul says there is only one, and it came “by revelation from Jesus Christ” (1:12).
Greek charis, a free gift to someone who has not earned it. ‘Justified freely by His grace’ (3:24).
Greek charis, a free gift and the goodwill behind it. In chapters 8 and 9 Paul uses it for God's kindness, for Christ's coming, and for the church's own giving (8:1, 8:6-9).
Greek charis, God's free gift and the goodwill behind it. God called Paul “by His grace” (1:15). To add the law as a condition is to set it aside (2:21).
Greek charis, God's free gift and the goodwill behind it. “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith” (2:8).
Greek paidagōgos, a household slave who looked after a boy until he grew up. Paul's picture of the law's work “to lead us to Christ” (3:24).
Two Hebrew words: hallelu, ‘praise’, and Yah, a short form of God's name. ‘Praise the LORD.’ It frames each of the last five psalms.
The Hebrew yad, hand, meaning power and favor. The refrain says it was on Ezra (7:6, 9, 28) and on his company on the road (8:18, 22, 31).
Three Hebrew verbs: to make strong, to make heavy, and to make hard. The plague stories use all three of Pharaoh's heart (4:21; 7:14).
In Hebrew the center of thought, will and loyalty, not only of feeling. Samuel was told that ‘the LORD sees the heart’ (16:7).
The inner self that thinks, chooses and loves. The Spirit writes on “tablets of human hearts” (3:3), and Paul pleads, “Open wide your hearts also” (6:13).
Greek splanchna, the inner parts, the seat of the deepest feelings (verses 7, 12, 20).
The unseen world where Christ reigns and where the powers of evil still act (1:3, 20; 6:12).
The Hebrew word behind ‘devote them to complete destruction’: a city and its people given over wholly, with no plunder kept (7:2; 20:17).
The Hebrew word for the ban: a city and its people given over wholly to God, with no plunder kept for the victors (6:17).
Greek spilas, a rock under the water that wrecks ships; some read ‘stains’ (1:12).
In Hebrew bamah, local hilltop shrines (3:2). In Kings they become a mark of failure, even under good kings (15:14).
In Hebrew bamah, local hilltop shrines. Even good kings left them, until Hezekiah removed them (18:4).
The priest who once a year entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. Jesus is the great high priest (4:14).
Greek periousios, found only here. God's word for Israel at Sinai (2:14; Exodus 19:5).
Being set apart for God, in body and in conduct. ‘For it is God’s will that you should be holy’ (4:3).
Hebrew qadosh: set apart for God and belonging to him. God is holy, and he calls his people to be holy (11:44; 19:2).
God's own Spirit, who fills people to speak, rests on Jesus, and is promised to the disciples (3:22, 24:49).
God's own Spirit, promised by Jesus and poured out at Pentecost (1:5, 2:4, 2:33). In Acts the Spirit gives courage and guides the church.
The Hebrew miqveh. After Ezra's prayer of utter guilt, it is a layman, Shecaniah, who says ‘there is hope for Israel’ (10:2).
The name this book usually gives to Mount Sinai, where God spoke the Ten Commandments (1:2; 5:2).
The appointed time of Jesus' death, rising and return to the Father. ‘Not yet’ at first, then ‘it has come’ (2:4, 12:23).
In Hebrew bayit: a building, a palace, a temple, a household or a line of kings. David offers to build God a house, and God promises to build David one (7:11).
In Hebrew bayit: a building, a palace, a temple or a line of kings. Solomon builds the LORD's house, and God keeps his promise of a house for David.
Small figures kept in a home and perhaps used to seek guidance, called teraphim in Hebrew. Micah kept them in his shrine (17:5).
A small figure kept in a home, called teraphim in Hebrew. Michal laid one in David's bed to fool Saul's men (19:13).
From the Greek word for a stage actor: someone whose religion is a mask (6:2, 23:13).
Greek eidōlon, an image of a god, and any false object of worship. The letter's last word (5:21).
Greek eikōn. Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (1:15), and believers are renewed in the image of their Creator (3:10).
Hebrew for ‘God with us’ (1:23). The promise the book closes on (28:20).
Greek euthys, Mark's favourite word, about forty times. It sets the pace (1:10, 1:12).
Belonging to Christ and sharing his life. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (5:17).
Joined to Christ, sharing his life. The phrase, with ‘in Him’, runs all through chapter 1: every blessing is found there (1:3).
The words that open the last chapters, with the refrain that there was no king in Israel (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25).
A family's share of the land, handed down through the generations and received as a gift from God (13:7).
In Hebrew nachalah, a family's land held from God down the generations. Naboth would not sell his (21:3).
Greek paideuō, the word for bringing up a child. Grace is the teacher (2:12).
The new name given to Jacob ‘because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed’ (32:28). It became the name of his whole people.
The Hebrew name Yehoshua, which means that the LORD saves. In Greek it is Iesous, the same word as the name Jesus.
Greek chara and chairō. Gladness rooted in the Lord, not in circumstances. “Rejoice in the Lord always” (4:4).
The Hebrew shophet: a leader God raised up to rescue his people and set things right, more often a deliverer than a judge in court (2:16).
Greek dikaioō, to set in the right, to declare in the right, a word from the law court. A person is justified “by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16).
Greek dikaioō, a law-court word: to declare someone in the right. God ‘justifies the wicked’ who trust him (4:5). Churches differ on what more it includes.
Greek dikaioō, to declare righteous or to show to be righteous. Readers differ on which James means (2:21-25).
The oasis on the southern edge of Canaan where the scouts reported, the people refused the land, and Miriam died (13:26; 20:1).
The gold cover of the ark, called the mercy seat in English Bibles, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (16:14).
Glory, from a root meaning ‘heavy’ or ‘weighty’. The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (40:34).
Greek tēreō, to keep, guard or hold. It frames the letter (1:1, 6, 13, 21).
The Berean Standard Bible's word in 2:12 for the Hebrew chesed, loyal love that keeps its word. Rahab shows it and asks for it.
The Hebrew chesed: love that keeps faith and goes beyond duty. The Berean Standard Bible also says loving devotion (1:8; 2:20; 3:10).
God's rule, God putting the world right. It comes near in Jesus (1:15).
God's rule, God putting the world right. It comes near in Jesus (10:9) and is ‘in your midst’ (17:21).
God's rule, God putting the world right. Matthew's way of saying ‘kingdom of God’; used about thirty times (4:17, 5:3).
In Hebrew go'el: a near relative with the right and duty to buy back family land, free a relative or take up a family's cause (2:20; 3:9).
To make atonement. The word has been linked with covering, with wiping clean and with a ransom that spares a life (4:20; 16:30).
Greek gnōsis. The Corinthians prized it. Paul does not despise it, but says “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1).
Greek epignōsis, full or personal knowledge: knowing God and Jesus, which bears fruit in life (1:2-3, 8; 3:18).
Christ, slain and standing at the centre of the throne (5:6).
A prayer that brings grief, complaint or protest straight to God. About a third of the psalms are laments. It is complaint that stays addressed to God.
A picture of a family line kept alive. God kept a lamp for David in Jerusalem through kings who did not deserve it (11:36; 15:4).
A picture of a family line kept alive. The LORD had promised to maintain a lamp for David (8:19).
The seven churches (1:12, 20).
In the New Testament, the whole time between Christ's first coming and his return (3:1).
Two words stand side by side in the king's letter: the law of God, and dat, a Persian word for a king's decree (7:26).
Greek nomos. Usually the law God gave Israel through Moses: holy and good (7:12), but unable to set a person right with God or free from sin (3:20, 8:3).
Greek nomos. In Galatians usually the law God gave through Moses at Sinai, 430 years after the promise to Abraham (3:17). God's good gift, but not the gate into his family.
Hebrew torah. More than rules: God's teaching or instruction. Psalm 1 calls it a delight, and Psalm 119 praises it from A to Z.
Greek anomia: sin as refusing God's rightful rule, not only breaking a rule (3:4).
In Hebrew nagid, the title God gives Saul (9:16) and later the man after his own heart (13:14): a ruler appointed by God and answerable to him.
In Hebrew tsara'at, a range of skin diseases, not only what is called leprosy today. Naaman had it (5:1), and so did four men at Samaria's gate (7:3).
A member of the tribe of Levi, set apart for service at the sanctuary and given towns instead of a share of land (17:7).
The tribe set apart to carry and guard the tabernacle. They camped between the tent and the other tribes (1:50-53).
Raised on a cross, and raised high in honour, both at once (3:14, 12:32-33).
God's truth and goodness shining into a dark world. Jesus calls himself the light of the world (1:5, 8:12).
God's holiness and truth, with no darkness at all; to walk in it is to live honestly before him (1:5-7).
Jesus' gentle rebuke to followers who trust him, but not enough to stop being afraid (8:26, 14:31).
How the prophets named the LORD over against idols, which cannot speak or act (1:9; Jeremiah 10:10).
Hope that rests on the resurrection of Jesus and looks to an inheritance that cannot spoil (1:3-4).
Christ, rejected by people but chosen by God; believers too are living stones in his house (2:4-5).
Small capitals stand for God's personal name in Hebrew, often written Yahweh (Exodus 3:14-15). ‘Lord’ in ordinary letters is a different word, meaning ‘master’.
The name given to Jesus, the name Isaiah gives to Israel's God. Every tongue will confess “that Jesus Christ is Lord” (2:11).
God's personal name, four Hebrew letters probably said ‘Yahweh’. English Bibles print it LORD in small capitals. It first appears in 2:4.
God's personal name, four Hebrew letters probably said ‘Yahweh’. English Bibles print it LORD in small capitals. Its meaning is opened in 3:14-15.
God as commander of all powers, the armies of heaven and of Israel. First Samuel is the first book of the Bible to use the title (1:3).
Sunday, the day of the resurrection (1:10).
Those who have wandered from God, like a sheep, a coin or a son (chapter 15). Jesus came to seek them (19:10).
The way the land was divided, so that the choice was left with God and not with the strongest tribe (14:2; 18:10).
Greek agapē, love that seeks another's good at cost to itself. Without it every gift is nothing (13:1-3). Of faith, hope and love, “the greatest of these is love” (13:13).
Greek agapē, self-giving love, defined by God sending his Son (4:7-10).
Greek agapē, defined as walking in God's commands (1:5-6).
The church's shared meals, often with the Lord's Supper (1:12).
Greek philanthrōpia, the root of ‘philanthropy’, a virtue praised in kings. Here it is God's (3:4).
Greek philoprōteuō, found only here in the New Testament: hunger for first place (1:9).
The Berean Standard Bible's words for the Hebrew chesed, love that keeps its promises (7:9).
The Hebrew chesed: loyal, covenant-keeping love. Jonathan asks David never to cut it off from his household (20:14-15).
The Hebrew chesed: loyal, covenant-keeping love. God promises it will never be removed from David's son as it was from Saul (7:15).
The Hebrew chesed: faithful, covenant-keeping love, even to the unfaithful. The singers praise it as the foundation is laid (3:11).
The Hebrew chesed: God's faithful covenant love. Nehemiah's first prayer begins with the God ‘who keeps His covenant of loving devotion’ (1:5).
Hebrew hesed. God's loyal, faithful love, kept because he bound himself by promise. The Berean Standard Bible often says ‘loving devotion’. It appears 127 times in the Psalms.
Greek teleioō, to complete, to bring to the goal. Never a hint that Jesus was once sinful (2:10; 5:9).
Priestly wise men from Persia and nearby lands who studied the stars and dreams (2:1).
A prophet, someone sent with God's word. The widow of Zarephath calls Elijah one (17:24).
A prophet, someone sent with God's word. Elisha is called this again and again, and the woman of Shunem calls him a holy man of God (4:9).
A figure who sets himself above every god (2:3-4). Who he is has been read in several ways; none is certain.
The bread God gave each morning in the wilderness. The people grew tired of it and longed for the food of Egypt (11:4-9).
Bitter. Naomi, whose name means pleasant, asks to be called Mara when she comes home (1:20).
Greek despotēs, the owner of a slave. Christ is the Master who bought his people (2:1).
Greek despotēs, a word often used of God; here of Jesus Christ (1:4).
Greek mesitēs, a go-between who brings two sides together. ‘One mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus’ (2:5).
A person who claimed to call up the dead, forbidden by the law of Moses. Saul had removed them from the land and then sought one out (28:3, 7).
Greek apantēsis. Often used when a city's people went out to welcome an arriving ruler and escort him back in (4:17).
King of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14). His name means ‘king of righteousness’ (7:2).
Shown to those who doubt, and to others with care (1:2, 21-23).
‘Quarreling’, the name given to the waters where Israel quarreled with the LORD and Moses struck the rock (20:13).
‘Anointed one’ in Hebrew and in Greek: the king God promised to send (1:1, 16:16).
The thousand years of 20:1-6, read in several ways.
Greek phroneō, to think, set your mind, hold an attitude. “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (2:5).
Greek diakonia, service. Paul's word for his own work and for the collection. It is the word for a servant's work, not a ruler's (3:6-9; 9:12).
The tabernacle, from the verb ‘to dwell’. The tent where God lived among his people (25:8-9).
The land east of the Dead Sea, home of Ruth and of Orpah, often at odds with Israel (1:1-4).
Greek dei, it is necessary. Luke's word for God's plan: the Son of Man must suffer and rise (9:22, 24:7).
Greek mystērion, a secret once hidden and now made known by God: that Gentiles are “fellow heirs” with Israel in Christ (3:6).
A secret of God now made known: “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27).
The temple is ‘a house for the Name of the LORD my God’ (5:5): God truly present there, yet never contained (8:27).
In the Bible a name stands for the person and his authority. Acts heals, baptizes and preaches ‘in the name of Jesus’ (3:6, 4:12).
The name of Jesus, for whose sake the workers went out (1:7).
Greek psychikos, a person living only by human powers, without the Spirit (2:14). Not wicked in itself, but unable to receive what the Spirit gives.
A man or woman set apart to God for a time by a vow: no wine, no cutting of the hair, no contact with the dead (6:1-21).
A person set apart to God by a vow: no wine, no razor, no touching the dead (Numbers 6). Samson was one from the womb (13:5).
The name later given to the bronze snake Moses made. It had become an idol, and King Hezekiah broke it up (21:9; 2 Kings 18:4).
The bronze snake Moses made, which the people had turned into an idol. Hezekiah broke it up (18:4).
Greek palingenesia, becoming again. In Matthew 19:28 it names the renewal of all things (3:5).

A covenant is a binding promise between God and his people. God promised a new one through Jeremiah, written on hearts. Paul is a servant “of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (3:6).
The son of Ruth and Boaz, the father of Jesse and grandfather of David (4:17).
The burnt offering, from the verb ‘to go up’. The whole gift went up to God in smoke (1:3-9).
The life before Christ and the life made new in him, put off and put on like clothes (4:22-24).
Greek ephapax, once and never again. Christ's sacrifice does not need repeating (7:27; 9:12; 10:10).
A common slave name meaning ‘useful’ or ‘beneficial’, the kind of name an owner gave (verse 10).
The Hebrew tseaqah, the cry of the oppressed that God hears, as Israel cried out in Egypt. The poor raise it in 5:1.
Where unclean things were taken in Israel's wilderness camp, and where Jesus suffered, outside the city gate (13:12-13).
Greek nikaō, to conquer, as the Lamb did, by faithful witness (2:7; 12:11).
Greek episkopos, one who watches over. Later the word for bishop; in this letter a local church leader, it seems the same person as an elder (3:1).
Leaders of the church in Philippi (1:1). Overseer later became the word for bishop; deacon means servant.
The Hebrew pardes, a Persian word for an enclosed park, here the king's forest (2:8). Its Greek form later gave English the word paradise.
A Persian word for a garden; used for the place of the righteous dead with God (23:43).
The word for a ruler's arrival on an official visit. Paul uses it for the return of Jesus (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23).
Used of Christ's coming (2:1) and, as a dark copy, of the lawless one's (2:9). The counterfeit is no match.
Greek koinonia, a shared life and common cause. The Philippians shared in Paul's work by prayer, gifts and help (1:5).
Greek koinōnia, shared life, shared faith, even shared debt (verses 6, 17).
The Hebrew phrase behind the BSB's sacrificed in the fire (16:3; 21:6). Most scholars read it as child sacrifice, which the prophets call innocent blood.
Greek makrothumia, being ‘long-tempered’: bearing people and hardship without giving up or hitting back (5:7-10).
Greek makrothumeō, to be long-tempered: holding back from anger to give time to turn (3:9, 15).
Not only calm, but enemies made friends. Christ “is our peace” (2:14), making Jews and Gentiles one.
Greek for ‘fiftieth’. The Jewish Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when the Spirit came (2:1).
Passover, from the Hebrew verb meaning to pass over (12:13). The feast that remembers the night God spared Israel's houses.
In that world, a whole way of life, not only argument. Paul warns against one built on human tradition (2:8).

words.word: The place the LORD will choose

entries.line: The phrase Deuteronomy uses for the one sanctuary where Israel is to worship. The book never names it (12:5).
Greek arrabōn, a first payment that promises the rest will follow. God has given “the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come” (5:5; also 1:22).
In Luke, people with little money and little power, often the ones who know they need God (4:18, 6:20).
Greek hierateuma, a body of priests. Peter gives Israel's title to the whole church (2:5, 9).
God's word to Abraham that the nations would be blessed through him. The law “does not revoke” it (3:17). In Christ it reaches the Gentiles.
A Gentile who has fully joined the Jewish people; the BSB says ‘convert to Judaism’ (2:11, 6:5).
Greek euodoō, first ‘to have a good road’, so to go well. Not a word about money (1:2).
Greek physioō, to inflate. A favourite word of this letter for the church's swollen pride (4:6; 5:2; 8:1; 13:4).
Like changing clothes: the old self taken off, the new self put on, and over all, love (3:9-14).
An offering, from the Hebrew verb ‘to come near’. To bring an offering was to draw near to God (1:2).
An Assyrian title, a chief officer, not a name. He mocked Hezekiah's trust outside Jerusalem's wall (18:17-35).
Greek apaugasma, brightness shining out from a source. The Son is the shining of God's own glory (1:3).
To keep a dead man's family line and his share of the land alive through a son (4:5, 4:10).
The price paid to set a captive free. Jesus says he gives his life as one (10:45).
A price paid to set others free. Christ ‘gave Himself as a ransom for all’ (2:6).
Greek apostasia, revolt or falling away. A great rebellion against God before the Day (2:3).
Greek katallagē, making friends again after a quarrel. In Paul, God is the one who reconciles and people are reconciled to him: “Be reconciled to God” (5:20).
A handwritten note of what someone owed. God cancelled it, “nailing it to the cross” (2:14).
Greek lutroō, to set free by paying a price, as a slave or captive was freed (1:18-19).
Greek apolutrōsis, setting free by paying a price, as a slave or prisoner was freed. Believers are justified ‘through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus’ (3:24).
A place to run to and hide, like a rock shelter in the hills. ‘Take refuge in’ God means to trust him for safety (2:12; 7:1).
Greek thrēskeia, the outward practice of worship. James says what God counts as pure religion (1:26-27).
Greek menō, to stay, abide or remain: John's word for a settled, lasting bond with God (2:24, 27-28).
The great duty of the book: to keep in mind the slavery in Egypt, the rescue, and the years in the wilderness (5:15; 8:2).
The Hebrew zakar: to bring to mind in a way that leads to action. Nehemiah asks God to remember his word (1:8), to remember Nehemiah (5:19; 13:31), and to remember his enemies (6:14).
Those who are left after judgment. Isaiah promised that a remnant would go out from Jerusalem (19:30-31).
The Hebrew peletah, those who escaped. Ezra's prayer calls the returned community a remnant spared by grace (9:8, 15).
To turn around: a change of mind that changes the direction of a life (1:4, 1:15).
Greek metanoeō, to change one's mind and turn one's life around (2:38, 3:19).
Greek metanoeō, to change mind and direction (2:5).
Greek metanoia, a change of mind and life. Preached by John (3:3) and sent to all nations (24:47).
A home in the land and an end of war, promised by Moses and given under Joshua (1:13; 21:44). Hebrews 4 speaks of a greater rest still open.
The years of peace after a deliverance: forty, eighty, forty and forty (3:11; 3:30; 5:31; 8:28). After Gideon the land is never again said to have rest.
Greek katapausis, the rest God gives; and sabbatismos, a Sabbath rest, a word found only here in the Bible (4:9).
Greek katechō, to hold back. Paul speaks of ‘what’ restrains and then ‘the one who’ restrains (2:6-7).
Greek anastasis, the rising of the dead to bodily life. Christ is “the firstfruits” (15:20), the first of the harvest; those who belong to him will follow.
Greek apokalupsis, unveiling. Jesus is Lord now, though hidden; his coming will unveil it (1:7).
Greek apokalupsis, an unveiling: a curtain drawn back (1:1).
Hebrew tsaddiq. Not people who never sin, but those who belong to God, trust him and seek his ways. Their opposite is ‘the wicked’.
Living rightly before God and with others; more a heart made new than a list of rules (5:6, 5:20, 6:33).
Greek dikaiosynē, being in the right. ‘The righteousness of God’ (1:17) may mean the right standing God gives, God's own saving faithfulness, or both.
In Hebrew tsur, a crag that gives shelter. David's song calls God his rock (22:2-3), and his last words call God ‘the Rock of Israel’ (23:3).
In Hebrew nagid, a leader appointed by God (5:2; 7:8). David's authority is given to him; the people remain God's.
Spiritual powers opposed to God. Christ is seated far above them (1:21), and the church makes God's wisdom known to them (3:10).
To go beyond the teaching of Christ, as if to a higher faith (1:9).
The seventh day of rest, named ten times in chapter 13. Nehemiah shuts the gates to keep it holy (13:19-22).
Greek hagioi, holy ones, people set apart for God. Paul calls the whole troubled church “called to be holy” (1:2). It is not a word for the unusually good.
To make holy. Paul prays that the God of peace will sanctify them ‘completely’, the whole person (5:23).
The council of leading priests, elders and teachers of the law in Jerusalem, led by the high priest (4:15, 5:21).
Greek sōtēr. One who rescues. The angels call Jesus ‘a Savior’ (2:11); Roman cities gave the same title to the emperor.
Mockers who follow their own desires, as the apostles foretold (1:18).
The Hebrew sopher: an official in charge of documents (4:8), and in Ezra a scholar and teacher of the law of Moses (7:6).
An older word for a prophet, one who sees: ‘the prophet of today was formerly called the seer’ (9:9).
A word at the end of a line, 71 times in the Psalms. Probably a direction for singing or music. Its exact meaning is not known.
Greek sōphrōn, a sound, steady mind that rules its desires. Asked of every group in chapter 2.
Greek propempō, to supply a traveller for the next stage of the trip (1:6).
The Hebrew badal, to separate, the verb of Genesis 1. Outsiders separated themselves from impurity to join Israel (6:21), and the men are told to separate from the peoples of the land (10:11).
Food laws and holy days are “a shadow of the things to come” (2:17); the reality is Christ.
The peace offering, related to shalom, peace or well-being. The one sacrifice the worshiper ate (3:1; 7:11-18).
‘Hear’, the first Hebrew word of 6:4, and the name of the confession Jews recite evening and morning (6:4-9).
‘Names’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first words: “These are the names of the sons of Israel” (1:1).
The Hebrew name for the place of the dead, pictured as dark and silent, below the earth. In the New Testament's Greek it becomes Hades (Acts 2:27).
A word for a king across the ancient world. The LORD told David, ‘You will shepherd My people Israel’ (5:2).
The word the men of Gilead used at the fords to tell an Ephraimite by his speech (12:6).
The town in the hill country where the Tent of Meeting was set up and the last of the land was shared out (18:1).
John's word for Jesus' miracles: deeds that point beyond themselves to who he is. John records seven in his first half (2:11, 20:30).
The Latin form of the name Silas, Paul's companion on this trip (Acts 15:40). He is named first after Paul (1:1).
Greek hamartia. Wrong acts, and also a power that rules people like a master and pays its wages in death (6:23).
The golden calves at Bethel and Dan, which every northern king kept, even Jehu (10:29).
Greek doulos, a person owned by another. Onesimus returns ‘no longer as a slave’ (verse 16).
A gentle way of speaking of death, in Jewish and Greek speech alike. For Christians it means those who sleep will wake (4:13-15).
A title for the promised king from David's family. Matthew uses it more than any other Gospel (1:1, 21:9).
Who Jesus is, said by the narrator, by God's voice, by demons, and at last by a Roman soldier (1:1, 1:11, 15:39).
Jesus' favourite name for himself, from Daniel 7:13-14: a human figure given an everlasting kingdom (16:27-28, 26:64).
Jesus' name for himself, from Daniel 7: the figure given an everlasting kingdom, who in Mark must suffer first (2:10, 8:31).
Jesus' favourite name for himself, from Daniel 7:13; one who serves, suffers and will come in glory (19:10, 21:27).
Groups of prophets who lived and worked together around a senior prophet such as Elijah or Elisha (2:3; 4:38).
Hebrew nephesh. Not a ghostly part of a person but the whole living self: life, breath, desire. ‘My soul’ often simply means ‘I’.
Healthy. Teaching that makes people well (1:9, 13; 2:1-2).
Greek hugiainō, to be healthy. Teaching that makes people spiritually well (1:10; 6:3).
In Hebrew ruach: spirit, wind or breath. Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's (2:9), the share of the firstborn heir.
Greek pneuma. God's Holy Spirit, who gives life, makes believers God's children, and helps them in weakness (8:11, 8:15, 8:26).
God's own Spirit, given when the Galatians heard and believed (3:2). The Spirit makes believers God's children and grows the fruit of a new life (5:22).

words.word: The Spirit of the LORD came upon

entries.line: God's power given to a judge for a task. The book never mistakes the gift for good character (3:10; 14:6).
God's power coming suddenly and strongly on a person for a task, on Saul (10:10; 11:6) and on David (16:13).

Greek pneumatikos, shaped by the Spirit of God. The Corinthians used it to rank themselves. Paul says the truly spiritual person has the Spirit, and that their quarrels show they are not living like it (3:1-3).
Greek stoicheia: the elements, first lessons, or the powers some thought ruled them (2:8, 20).
Greek oikonomos, the manager of a household for its owner. Leaders do not own the church; they manage it for God (1:7).
Greek oikonomos, a household manager who handles what belongs to another (4:10).
The Hebrew ur, to rouse, as one wakes a sleeper. The LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus (1:1) and of everyone who goes up to build (1:5).
The Hebrew chazaq, to be strong. The people strengthen their hands for the work (2:18), and the same verb is the word for repairing the wall, again and again in chapter 3.

The Hebrew darash, to seek or inquire. Ezra set his heart to seek, that is to study, the law of the LORD (7:10). Later Jewish tradition took its word midrash, interpretation of Scripture, from this root.
Greek hypotassō, to place oneself under, to defer. Asked first of all believers toward one another (5:21).
The Greek name for the deepest prison of the underworld, used for where the angels who sinned are held (2:4).
Greek didachē. ‘The teaching of Christ’: about Christ, or given by him (1:9-10).
The small cases, worn on the body or fixed to the doorframe, in which Jewish tradition keeps the words of 6:4-9.
In Hebrew netinim, those given: workers given to the temple's service. They came home, and they are listed by family (2:43; 8:20).
The tabernacle, the tent at the center of the camp where God lived among his people and spoke with Moses (1:1; 2:2).
Greek marturia, evidence given to show what is true. God's witness about his Son (5:9-11).
Greek marturia, open witness to a person's character (1:12).
A ruler of part of a kingdom under Rome, such as Herod Antipas in Galilee (3:1, 3:19).
The man Luke writes to; the name means ‘friend of God’ (1:3, Acts 1:1).
A flat, open place where grain was tossed into the breeze to blow the chaff away. Owners slept beside the grain to guard it (3:2).
In Hebrew goren, an open place for separating grain from chaff. Araunah's floor became the site of David's altar (24:18-25) and later of the temple.
A phrase the book uses of stones, names and families that were still there when it was written (4:9; 6:25; 7:26).
A word Moses uses constantly. Every generation that hears the book is addressed as if it stood at the Jordan (5:3; 30:15).
Greek sēmeron. Luke's word for the moment God's promise arrives (2:11, 4:21, 19:9, 23:43).
‘Formless and void’ (1:2): a world empty and without order, not yet fit to live in. The days of creation shape it and then fill it.
‘Generations’ or ‘account’, from the verb ‘to give birth’. ‘This is the account of’ opens each main section of Genesis; the word appears 13 times in the book.
Hebrew for instruction or teaching. It is the name Jews give to the five books of Moses.
Greek paradosis, what is handed on. Here the apostles' own teaching, by speech or by letter (2:15; 3:6).
Greek peirasmos, a test from outside or a pull to sin from within. The same hardship can lead either way (1:2, 12-14).
Greek thlipsis, pressure, being pressed hard. Paul uses it of his own hardships, and pairs it with comfort. God comforts “in all our troubles” (1:4), not by taking every trouble away.
Paul's mark for a saying of the early church that he quotes and stands behind (1:15; 3:1; 4:9).
A saying of the early church that Paul quotes and stands behind (2:11).
Greek alētheia, God's reality shown in Christ, which abides in believers (1:1-4).
Greek alētheia. Gaius walks in it; the workers serve it (1:3-4, 8).
The skin disease of chapters 13 and 14, once translated leprosy. It covers several conditions, and even mildew in cloth and walls.
Image. Kings set up images of themselves to show their rule. Genesis says every human being, male and female, is made in God's image (1:27).
Greek epistrephō, to turn around. The Thessalonians ‘turned to God from idols’ (1:9). Conversion is a change of direction.
Hebrew tame: not fit, for a time, to come near the holy place. A ritual state, not dirt and not the same as sin (chapters 11 to 15).
Mark's usual name for a demon, an evil power that harms people and fears Jesus (1:23, 5:2).
The Hebrew bin. It runs through chapter 8: those who could understand, the Levites helping them understand, and the people rejoicing because they understood (8:2, 8, 12).
Solomon's request (3:9), in Hebrew literally a hearing heart: one that listens to God and to the people it must judge.
Greek ataktōs, out of order, like a soldier out of rank. Living outside the way the church had been taught (3:6, 11).
The Hebrew maal, breaking faith with someone owed loyalty. Ezra 9 and 10 use it to name what the marriages meant (9:2; 10:10).
One of the two sacred lots, with the Thummim, used to put a question to the LORD (14:41; 28:6).
Greek achrēstos and euchrēstos. Paul's play on the name, which may also have sounded like Christos (verse 11).
‘And he called’, the Hebrew name of the book, from its first word (1:1).
Greek aretē, excellence or goodness, a favourite word of Greek moral teaching (1:3, 5).
Hebrew qavah. Not idle waiting, but looking to God in hope, like a watchman waiting for the morning (130:5-6).
Paul's word for how a person lives day by day. “walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received” (4:1).
Stars off course, useless to sailors who steered by them (1:13).
The road to Jerusalem, and the life of following Jesus on it (1:2-3, 8:27, 10:52).
An early name for the followers of Jesus and their way of life (9:2, 19:9, 24:14).
Greek astheneia, frailty, sickness, lack of strength. The world's reason to despise Paul, and the place of Christ's power: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10).
The Persian province of which Judah was a small part, the lands beyond the river as seen from Persia (4:10; 5:3).
The faith handed to Timothy to guard, like money left with a trusted friend (6:20).
Greek parathēkē, a deposit left in trust. The gospel given to Timothy to guard (1:14).
The Hebrew kanaph means a wing or the corner of a garment. Ruth shelters under God's wings (2:12) and asks for the corner of Boaz's garment (3:9).
In Hebrew chokmah, skill for living, from craftsmanship to governing to moral judgment. God gave it to Solomon as a gift (4:29).
Greek sophia. Corinth's wisdom meant clever speech, learning and status. God's wisdom is the crucified Christ, who “has become for us wisdom from God” (1:30).
Greek martus. One who tells what he has seen. The apostles are witnesses of the risen Jesus (1:8, 1:22); the word later came to mean martyr.
Greek martus, one who testifies; later, a martyr (1:5; 2:13).
Greek logos. God's speech, by which the world was made; in John, a name for the Son, who was with God and was God (1:1, 1:14).
The Hebrew melakhah, used for the rebuilding throughout. The enemies want to stop the work, and the people keep returning to it (4:6; 6:3).
Deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses (3:20, 3:28). Read as any effort to earn standing with God, or above all as the marks of being Jewish, such as circumcision.
Deeds the law of Moses requires. Read as any effort to earn God's favour, or above all as the marks of Jewish identity such as circumcision. See the part above.
Greek erga, things done. For James, deeds of faith and mercy, like feeding the hungry (2:14-26).
Often in John, people organized against God. Yet it is the world God loves (3:16, 15:18).
Greek sarkikos, living by merely human ways. Paul says jealousy and quarrels show it: “Are you not walking in the way of man?” (3:3).
God's settled opposition to evil, which will come on the Day of the Lord. Jesus is ‘our deliverer from the coming wrath’ (1:10).
Sea of reeds, the Hebrew name English Bibles give as the Red Sea (13:18). Where Israel crossed is not known.
Every seventh year, when debts were cancelled and the law was read aloud to all Israel (15:1-2; 31:10-11).
The beam that bound an animal to its work, and a picture of a king's demands. Rehoboam promised a heavier one (12:14).
The ram's horn, and so the Jubilee, the fiftieth year announced by its blast (25:9-10).
Seed or offspring. Like ‘seed’ in English it can mean one child or a whole line. It runs from 3:15 through every promise to Abraham's family.
First the Jebusite fortress David captured (5:7), then the City of David, the temple hill, Jerusalem, and God's people.
The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood, and so a name for Jerusalem and for God's dwelling among his people. It appears 38 times in the Psalms.
